d.title: The off-topic sentence outscores two of the three on-topic ones
d.caption: *“The weather that week was unremarkable”* scores **1.7321 — above the sentence about attention (1.6014)** — because `weather` and `unremarkable` are rare in this document and rarity is all the scorer measures. **TF-IDF cannot tell distinctive from relevant.** And length is the other structural bias: **summing over terms means a long sentence accumulates more weight than a short one saying the same thing**, so raw sums quietly favour verbosity, and dividing by length over-rewards one exotic word.

d.title: Seven times the parameters, five times the latency, two percent more compression
d.caption: `bart-large-cnn` has **406M parameters against t5-small's 61M and takes 115.2s against 23.1s** — and produces **60% compression against 58%**, on output that differs mainly in capitalisation. Which is worth measuring before choosing: **the big model's advantage here is not visible in either number this lesson can compute**, and §05 is about to show that neither output is doing what “abstractive” implies. Note the interface difference too: **T5 needs the `summarize: ` prefix and BART does not.**

d.title: Copy rate 100%, longest verbatim run 57 words, and no novel words at all
d.caption: Both outputs read well, **and on two of three inputs neither model produced a single word absent from the source.** The transcript case is the starkest: **33% shorter, and the entire 57-word output is one verbatim run.** Only the list of facts gives any novelty, and look at what it is — **`5.1million`, `6.8million`, `inq3`, `inq4`: artefacts of whitespace joining, not new wording.** So in practice **these models are doing high-quality extraction**, and the hallucination risk in §07 comes from the same mechanism occasionally not copying.

d.title: One substituted word, and the four variants disagree about how much it cost
d.caption: `sat` becomes `was`, and that single change costs **ROUGE-1 nothing in structure (0.8333) and ROUGE-2 a fifth of its score (0.6000)**, because the substitution breaks **two** bigrams while breaking only one unigram. ROUGE-L matches ROUGE-1 here because the LCS is still 5. **The orientation is the design choice: ROUGE is recall-first because the failure being penalised is omission** — a summary that leaves things out, not one that adds.

d.title: Six rows, and §05 just undercut one of them
d.caption: The table is the standard comparison and it is worth reading against this lesson's own measurement. **“Faithfulness: risk of hallucination” is the abstractive column's real cost — but §05 measured a 100% copy rate on two of three inputs, so in practice the models were faithful by accident rather than by construction.** The reliable differences are the other four: **extractive is milliseconds on CPU with no training data, and choppy between picks.**

d.title: Two families, and one of them needs to be told what language to emit
d.caption: **Marian/OPUS-MT is one small model per pair** — fast, CPU-friendly, hundreds of pairs published — against **M2M100's one model for 100 languages, any-to-any.** The multilingual one has a failure the per-pair one cannot have: **the decoder has to be told which language to produce, via a forced BOS token, and without it the model picks and often picks wrong.** Beam search is standard at **k = 4** for MT: keep the four best partial translations rather than the single best.

d.title: A good translation scores exactly zero, because one precision is zero
d.caption: *“the cat is on the mat”* against *“the cat sat on the mat”* is one word wrong and **`sentence_bleu` returns 0.0000** — because BLEU is a **geometric** mean, and a six-word candidate has only three 4-grams, none of which matches. **One zero in the product sets the whole score to zero**, which is why smoothing exists and lifts it to 0.2541. The practical consequence: **sentence-level BLEU is close to meaningless on short sentences, and BLEU is a corpus-level metric.**

d.title: At five words of nine, BLEU is the brevity penalty and nothing else
d.caption: **Every n-gram the five-word candidate emitted was correct, so all four precisions are 1.0 and BLEU equals BP exactly — 0.4493.** That is the penalty doing the entire job. **Without it, the translator's optimal strategy would be to emit the three words it was most confident about and stop**, scoring perfect precision on a useless output. Note how steep it is at the short end: **one word of nine gives BP 0.0003**, which is `e^(1−r/c)` behaving exponentially.

d.title: Seven bands, and the usable threshold is lower than people assume
d.caption: The bands are what a BLEU number means to a reader of the output, and **the interesting line is 20–29: the gist is clear with significant errors**, which is where a lot of deployed MT actually sits and is genuinely useful for triage. **Under 10 is useless and over 60 is often better than a human translation** — and that last band is also the one to distrust, since it usually means the test set overlaps the training data.

d.title: Two heads, and the null score is the one that decides whether to answer
d.caption: The architecture is an encoder with **two linear heads over `[CLS] question [SEP] passage [SEP]`** — one scoring each token as a start, one as an end — and **the answer is the span maximising the product, subject to the end not preceding the start.** The last two rows are the whole point: **on a question the passage cannot answer, the null score goes to 0.9981 and the model returns an empty string.** Abstention is a span too — the `[CLS]` position — which is what makes it expressible at all.

d.title: Fifty thousand unanswerable questions, and the model learns a different skill
d.caption: **SQuAD 1.1 guaranteed every question had an answer in its passage, so a model trained on it never learns to decline** — at inference it returns its best guess no matter what, **and a confident wrong span is far more dangerous than an abstention.** SQuAD 2.0's ~50,000 adversarially written unanswerable questions change what the model must learn: **not where the answer is, but whether there is one** — which moves abstention from an external confidence filter into the model's own output.
